talk: Money isn't free. Lenders want interest and owners want a return, and the blend of what they want is your cost of capital. A project is only worth doing if it earns more than that.

terms.meaning: The return lenders and owners expect for funding you.
The minimum return a project must beat.
Borrowed money, and money from owners who want a share of the profits.

questions.prompt: The club is funded by $6M of loans at 6% a year and $4M from owners who expect 16% a year. What's the blended cost of capital?
questions.hint: Work out the yearly cost of each in dollars, then divide by the total.
whyNot: 6% is only the loans. Owners' money costs 16%.
(6% + 16%) / 2 = 11% treats both as the same size. There's more loan money, so the blend leans toward 6%.
6% + 16% = 22% adds the rates together. Blend them by how much money each one provides.

questions.prompt: A new training ground costs $5M and should make $400,000 a year. Should you build it?
options: No, 8% is below the 10% cost of capital
questions.hint: Turn the profit into a yearly return and compare.
working: It shows a profit, but it earns less than the money costs.
whyNot: It does make $400,000 a year, but the $5M to build it costs $5M x 10% = $500,000 a year. You'd fall short.
The club isn't funded by loans alone. Owners' money costs 16%, so the blend, 10%, is the bar to beat.
Cost alone doesn't decide it. A $5M project would be worth it if it earned more than 10% a year.

questions.prompt: What yearly profit would the $5M training ground need just to match the cost of capital?
whyNot: $5M x 6% = $300,000 uses the loan rate. Owners' money costs more, so the blend is 10%.
$400,000 is what it's expected to make. That's below the bar.
$5M x 16% = $800,000 uses the owners' rate. The blended rate is 10%.

penalty.prompt: Loans of {debt} cost {dr} a year. Owners put in {eq} and expect {er} a year. What's the blended cost of capital, as a percentage?
penalty.hint: Yearly cost of each in dollars, added up, divided by the total money.
working: {debt * dr + eq * er|usd} / {debt + eq|usd} = {(debt * dr + eq * er) / (debt + eq)|pct}.

traps.why: That treats both as the same size. Weight each rate by how much money it provides.
That adds the rates together. Blend them by how much money each provides.

call.title: The training centre
call.prompt: A new training centre would be paid for with borrowed and owners' money, costing $10,000 a matchday. It should attract 400 more fans. A smaller version costs $5,000 a matchday and should attract 350.

options.label: Build the big one
options.result: 400 x $18 = $7,200 a matchday against $10,000 for the money. $7,200 - $10,000 = -$2,800 every matchday.

options.label: Build the smaller one
options.result: Good call. 350 x $18 = $6,300 against $5,000: $6,300 - $5,000 = $1,300 better off every matchday. It beats what the money costs.

options.label: Build nothing
options.result: Safe, but the smaller centre earns more than its money costs.

takeaway: A project has to beat what your money costs, not just break even.
